stories.headline: Justice Department moves to prosecute James Comey a third time
stories.summary: The Justice Department is trying for a third time to bring criminal charges against former FBI Director James Comey, this time alleging that he leaked classified national-defense information about a decade ago. Comey denies wrongdoing, and his lawyers say the case is legally invalid and was brought too late. Separately, a federal judge ruled that the department unlawfully fired his daughter, former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey.
stories.why_it_matters: Courts will now weigh whether a decade-old leak allegation can still be prosecuted, a test of how far the Justice Department can go in pursuing a longtime target of the president. Coverage came mostly from left-leaning and center outlets; three right-leaning outlets also reported the new charge.
stories.background: James Comey is a former FBI director and a longtime target of President Trump. The department's first case against him, brought in Virginia over his testimony to Congress, was dismissed by a judge, and he was later indicted in a separate case in North Carolina. In April, Bloomberg Government reported that prosecutors were also pursuing charges over alleged leaks of classified information. His lawyers say the newest case concerns a purported 2016 leak to The New York Times that was investigated years ago without charges.

facts.text: The Justice Department is seeking to prosecute Comey for a third time, alleging that he leaked classified national-defense information about 10 years ago.
Axios reported that the charging document was made public on Monday.
The New York Sun reported that the new charge is brought under the Espionage Act.
According to unsealed court documents, prosecutors claim Comey directed the leak while he was leading the FBI.

Comey's lawyers say the case centers on a purported leak of national security information to The New York Times in October 2016, an issue they say was already investigated and did not lead to charges.
Comey denies wrongdoing, and his lawyers argue the case is legally invalid and falls outside the time limit for bringing charges.
CBS News reported that the department took steps to bring the charge earlier this month; NBC News reported that Comey has not been indicted in the latest case.

The New York Times reported that the department has stepped up moves against Comey and others as the midterms near, and that in some cases court paperwork shows signs of urgency, such as typos and the signatures of senior political leadership.
In April, Bloomberg Government reported that the department was pursuing additional charges against Comey over alleged leaks of classified information, after he had been indicted in North Carolina.
Separately, a federal judge ruled that the department unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, James Comey's daughter, from her job as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan and ordered her reinstated.
Maurene Comey was fired in July 2025 and had handled the prosecutions of Jeffrey Epstein and Sean Combs.

stories.headline: Justice Dept. asks Washington to hold 400 voters' ballots as court lets California count 20,000
stories.summary: The Justice Department asked Washington state to set aside ballots from more than 400 people it alleges are registered to vote without U.S. citizenship, a week before the midterm elections. A federal appeals court separately declined the administration's request to stop California from counting the ballots of about 20,000 voters the department has challenged on the same grounds. President Trump also offered a $1 million reward for voter fraud tips that lead to convictions.
stories.why_it_matters: With Election Day a week away, the moves bear on whether some voters' ballots are counted and on how far federal officials can reach into vote counting that states run. Most of the coverage came from left-leaning outlets.
stories.background: States, not the federal government, handle counting ballots and certifying results. The Trump administration has pressed claims that noncitizens are voting: in July the Justice Department warned Washington election officials that they could face criminal liability for keeping noncitizens on voter rolls, and this month it sued California and Los Angeles County to stop the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 people that federal agencies flagged as likely noncitizens. Officials in both states have pushed back: Washington's secretary of state accused the department of trying to intimidate election officials, and California's said it had not supplied evidence for its figure. Prosecuted cases of illegal voting by noncitizens remain rare, according to statistics cited by NewsNation.

facts.text: The Justice Department on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges are registered to vote without U.S. citizenship.
Federal prosecutors said they sent a letter to Washington's secretary of state listing the 400 people.
The department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by those more than 400 people in prior elections.

A federal appeals court declined the administration's request to block California from counting the ballots of 20,000 registered voters the department claims are noncitizens, so those ballots can be counted for now.
The New York Times reported that the appeals court panel's vote was 2-1.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom accused Trump of an “assault on democracy.”

The department sued California and Los Angeles County this month to stop officials from counting ballots from more than 20,000 people that federal agencies flagged as “likely noncitizens” until their citizenship can be verified.
NBC News and The Guardian described the Washington request as the latest in a series of administration moves into ballot counting handled by states, including states with competitive midterm races.

In July, the department warned Washington election officials that they could be held criminally liable if they knowingly kept noncitizens on voter rolls; Washington's secretary of state called that letter part of “a troubling pattern of efforts to intimidate election officials.”
Washington's Republican Party chair called the 400 suspected noncitizen voters the “tip of the iceberg,” The Center Square reported.
The Washington Times reported that ICE is investigating 1,900 cases of suspected noncitizen voting.
Trump offered a $1 million reward for voter fraud tips that lead to convictions; it was unclear where the money would come from.
Prosecuted cases of illegal voting or fraud by immigrants who do not have the right to vote remain rare, statistics show, NewsNation reported.

stories.headline: A week out, Trump campaigns in Mississippi and Texas as poll shows Democrats ahead
stories.summary: With one week until the midterm elections, President Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi and Tuesday in Texas, where Republicans face competitive Senate races. The final NPR/PBS News/Marist poll before Election Day found Democrats with an 8-point lead among likely voters in the fight for Congress, though NPR flagged lagging enthusiasm among key groups.
stories.why_it_matters: The elections could shift control of Congress, which writes federal budgets and tax law and oversees the administration. Tens of millions of people have already voted.
stories.background: Midterm elections fall halfway through a president's term and can shift power in Washington and in statehouses. In deep-red Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom is challenging Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, and in Texas, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a competitive Senate race. Both contests have drawn late spending and visits from national figures. Polls have shown Republicans likely to do poorly, and Trump and the top Republicans in Congress have attacked such polls as fake.

facts.text: Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi for Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, part of a closing rally blitz that the AP said highlights Republicans' challenges.

Democrats are making a play for the Mississippi seat, where Scott Colom is the Democratic challenger; the race has drawn millions in last-minute spending and high-profile visits, including a rally by Kamala Harris.
Fox News reported that national Democrats have reserved $1.2 million in Mississippi ads for Colom.
At the Mississippi rally, Trump responded at length to former President Barack Obama's criticism of his White House renovations, saying Obama “wouldn't understand.”
On Tuesday Trump was scheduled to rally in Corpus Christi and Lubbock, Texas, for Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee, who faces Democrat James Talarico.
A Fox News poll found Paxton and Talarico tied at 49% in the Texas Senate race.
Speaking to reporters before the trip, Trump said he would respect the midterm results “if they're honest.”
The chief justice of the Texas Supreme Court endorsed Talarico.
The New York Times reported that Paxton has taken about 350 trips outside Texas since he was sworn in as attorney general, which has drawn campaign scrutiny.

Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio planned to greet a newly arrived tanker carrying Venezuelan crude in Texas, which Bloomberg called a bid to showcase supply a week before the elections; Trump said Venezuela sent him 1 million barrels of oil as a “gift.”
The final NPR/PBS News/Marist poll before Election Day found Democrats with an 8-point lead among likely voters in the fight for control of Congress.
NPR said lagging enthusiasm among key groups is one sign that Democratic gains may not come easily.
In the same poll, 40% of people said their family finances had gotten worse.
Tens of millions of voters have already cast ballots.

stories.headline: Supreme Court leaves Texas-Justice Dept. deal limiting pauses in deportation cases in place
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to intervene against an agreement between the Trump administration and Texas that cuts off a way for immigration judges to pause some deportation cases. Opponents called the deal collusive and had asked the justices to restore a Biden-era rule that gave judges that discretion.
stories.why_it_matters: Immigrants with pending cases, such as crime victims or witnesses seeking other relief, lose a route to having deportation proceedings put on hold. Only left-leaning and center outlets in the ingest covered the ruling.
stories.background: A 2024 rule let immigration judges suspend some deportation cases, for example while a crime victim or witness sought other relief. In June, Texas sued to overturn it, the Justice Department agreed that the rule should be set aside, and U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor entered a consent judgment vacating it. Baltimore, New Haven, Columbus and the group Centro Legal de la Raza tried to step in to defend the rule, but O'Connor ruled they lacked standing and the 5th Circuit declined to block the judgment, sending them to the Supreme Court.

facts.text: The Supreme Court on Tuesday left in force a settlement between the Trump administration and Texas that cuts off an avenue for pausing some deportations.
Immigrant advocates called the agreement “collusion” and had asked the justices to reinstate a Biden-era policy that gave immigration judges discretion.
The outcome means the administration can block immigration judges from closing or shelving deportation cases.
The 2024 rule let immigration judges pause some deportation cases, such as when a crime victim or witness is seeking relief.
After Texas sued in June, the Justice Department agreed that the rule should be set aside, and Judge Reed O'Connor entered a consent judgment vacating it.

O'Connor denied a request by Baltimore, New Haven, Columbus and Centro Legal de la Raza to join the case and defend the rule, finding they lacked standing, and the 5th Circuit declined to block the judgment.

An advisory from the Immigrant Legal Resource Center says immigration courts have read the decision broadly since June, using it to deny closures and terminations and to put already-closed cases back on the calendar.

stories.headline: Judge extends block on changes at D.C. public golf course Trump wants to overhaul
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes extended an order barring the Trump administration from cutting more trees or making other changes at Washington's East Potomac Park without notice. Reyes noted that the president's social media posts contradicted sworn testimony from government officials. Trump said the administration would appeal and that the renovation would still start next month.
stories.why_it_matters: The fight is over public parkland near the National Mall, and the order means the government must give notice before it closes or alters the course. It also tests how a court responds when officials' sworn testimony conflicts with the president's public statements.
stories.background: East Potomac Golf Links is a century-old public golf course in East Potomac Park, near the National Mall, and Trump has sought to overhaul it. The DC Preservation League sued over the plans; in May, Reyes declined to issue a restraining order but told the National Park Service to consult government lawyers before cutting more than 10 trees. More than 500 trees have since been felled, and Reyes has now extended her block on further work.

facts.text: Reyes extended an order barring the government from clearing more trees or making other alterations at East Potomac Park without proper notice.
The order requires the government to give notice before closing or altering the property.
Reyes noted that the president's social media posts contradicted the sworn testimony of multiple government officials.
CNN reported that the judge criticized the Justice Department for asking her to “disbelieve” Trump.
Reyes wrote that the court “does not speak for the trees” but “speaks only for the rule of law,” echoing an earlier line that she was “not the Lorax.”
More than 500 trees had been felled at East Potomac Golf Links before the halt, The Hindu reported.
Trump said the administration would appeal and that the renovation would still start next month; The Hindu put the planned start at Nov. 15.

The DC Preservation League brought the case; in May, Reyes declined to issue a temporary restraining order but told the National Park Service to discuss any plans to cut more than 10 trees with government lawyers first.

stories.headline: FBI searches Beverly Hills mansion in Eric Swalwell investigation
stories.summary: Federal agents searched a Beverly Hills mansion on Tuesday morning as part of the investigation into former Rep. Eric Swalwell, a California Democrat who resigned from Congress amid sexual misconduct allegations. The home is connected to Stephen Cloobeck, a billionaire developer and onetime Swalwell associate and donor. Swalwell has denied the allegations.
stories.why_it_matters: The federal investigation of a former member of Congress now reaches property tied to a onetime associate. Outlets across the political spectrum covered the search.
stories.background: Swalwell, a California Democrat, resigned from Congress amid a wave of sexual misconduct allegations, which he has denied. In August, according to a Reuters source, FBI agents seized his electronic devices at San Francisco International Airport and searched his home in Washington. Cloobeck, a wealthy developer, had been a Swalwell donor and associate.

stories.headline: Judge refuses to approve new charges against ex-FBI officials in Hunter Biden testimony case
stories.summary: A federal magistrate judge in Washington on Tuesday refused to approve a new criminal complaint against two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about the bureau's Hunter Biden investigations, and scolded prosecutors over how they have handled the case. CBS News reported that the new complaint was unsigned and unsworn and was filed hours before the two were due in court for a preliminary hearing.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling is a judge's rebuke of how the Justice Department is handling a politically charged prosecution brought shortly before the midterms, and it bears on whether and how the case goes forward. Outlets across the political spectrum covered it.
stories.background: In 2023, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, then senior officials of the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force, told the House Judiciary Committee that the task force had not been involved in the bureau's investigations of Hunter Biden, President Joe Biden's son. On Oct. 23, the Justice Department charged each with one count of making a false statement to Congress, saying records, communications and witness accounts contradict that testimony. Prosecutors brought the case by a criminal complaint signed by a magistrate judge rather than a grand jury indictment, and the officials' lawyers call it baseless and politically motivated. The task force was disbanded in February 2025.

facts.text: Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui on Tuesday refused to approve a new criminal complaint against two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about the Hunter Biden investigations.
The judge scolded the Justice Department over its handling of the case, which PBS News described as unorthodox.
The Washington Examiner reported that the judge faulted prosecutors for filing the new complaint without first securing judicial approval.
CBS News reported that the new, superseding complaint was unsigned and unsworn and was filed hours before the two were due in federal court in Washington for a preliminary hearing.
The two were first accused of lying when they testified to Congress in 2023 about their involvement in the Hunter Biden investigations.
They are Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, former senior officials of the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force; each was charged last week with one count of making a false statement to Congress.

The original complaint says both told the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 that the task force was not involved in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations; investigators say records, communications and witness accounts contradict that testimony.
Prosecutors brought the charges through a criminal complaint signed by a magistrate judge rather than an indictment voted by a grand jury.
Lawyers for the two have called the case baseless and politically motivated.
